Set counts and RIR descend on a periodized schedule: weeks 1–3 hold base volume (2 sets compound / 3 isolation), weeks 4–5 are your overload peak (3/4 sets): mesocycle research shows adding sets is the best-supported lever for hypertrophy, and week 6 is a deload, matching what most competitive strength/physique athletes already do.

Targets, phase & maintenance›
Cuts target a 0.5–1% bodyweight loss per week (~500 kcal/day deficit) to preserve muscle. Lean bulks target a 200–350 kcal/day surplus (~0.25–0.5 kg/week gain): bigger surpluses mostly add fat past that point. Protein is set near 1g per pound of bodyweight. Fat sits at 25% of calories, carbs fill the remainder. Push weeks (4–5) nudge calories up; deload nudges down.

Weekly calorie check & phase check›
Weekly calorie check
This compares your actual trend-weight change to what you've logged eating over the same stretch to back-calculate your real maintenance calories, the same idea behind adaptive trackers like MacroFactor, instead of relying only on the Mifflin-St Jeor estimate, which is commonly off by a few hundred calories for a real person. It needs roughly two weeks of fairly consistent weigh-ins and food logging before it has enough signal to say anything, and it never changes your target on its own, you decide whether to apply it.
Phase check
Reassessed every time you open this tab, using how your waist has tracked against your weight change since this phase started, compared to how that same ratio looked earlier in the phase. It's a directional signal from what you've logged, not a body-composition scan, treat "wrap up soon" as worth a look, not a verdict, and it updates automatically as new weigh-ins and measurements come in rather than locking in a one-time prediction.
Right now
The old "30-minute anabolic window" is outdated, research since (Aragon & Schoenfeld's nutrient-timing reviews) shows the practical window for protein/carbs after training is several hours wide, not a sharp cutoff, and total daily intake matters far more than exact timing. This still leans toward sooner rather than much later, especially if you trained without eating beforehand.

Maintenance & body stats›
Your maintenance
BMI only relates height to total weight, it cannot tell muscle from fat. A lean, muscular lifter routinely scores "overweight" or "obese" on BMI despite low body fat. Treat the category label as a population-level screening tool, not a verdict on your physique.

Log measurements›
Tape measurements
Scale weight alone can't tell muscle gain from fat gain during a lean bulk, or muscle loss from fat loss during a cut. A couple of tape measurements alongside weight, waist especially, give a second signal: a bulk where waist barely moves while weight climbs is a good sign; a cut where waist shrinks much slower than weight is a warning sign. All fields are optional, log whichever you have a tape for today. Waist and neck (plus hips for women), with your height, also give a body fat estimate using the U.S. Navy tape method: typically within about 3–4% of a lab scan for one reading, but much better at showing which way you're trending. Measure waist at the navel, neck just below the Adam's apple, hips at the widest point, same time of day.
Glutes: widest point of the butt, feet together. Hips: at the top of the hip bones. Shoulders: around the widest point, arms down. Arm, forearm, thigh and calf: widest point, same side each time.

Show date & target
This checks your timeline against the sustainable fat-loss rate from the sports-nutrition literature, 0.5–1% of bodyweight per week preserves muscle during a cut; going meaningfully faster raises the risk of losing muscle along with fat. It covers the diet-phase math only. Peak week (water, sodium, and carb manipulation in the final days) is a separate, highly individual process that benefits from an experienced coach, this tool won't tell you how to run it, and getting genuinely stage-lean for the first time is not something to navigate from an app alone.

Enter steps by hand · why steps matter
Why steps matter
Daily movement outside the gym is the biggest swing factor in how many calories you burn, and it quietly drops when you diet, often why fat loss stalls. Keeping steps steady matters more than hitting a big number. Cardio calories aren't added back to your food: your weekly calorie check already learns your real burn from the scale, so adding them would double count. Hard cardio can eat into leg recovery, so keep it easy or away from leg days.
This week's volume sets · target
Hard sets per muscle per week across your whole schedule. An exercise counts as 1 set for the muscle it targets and ½ a set for muscles it clearly helps with (rows → biceps, presses → triceps and front delts, squats → glutes), the way volume research counts it. The status is judged on your block's average week, base weeks are lighter and overload weeks heavier by design. Ranges come from Renaissance Periodization's volume landmarks and dose-response research, population averages, not hard rules. That's why your own feedback moves each muscle: a purple +1/−1 means sets were added or removed because of how that muscle recovered, pumped and performed. "Focus" marks a muscle you chose to bring up.
Optimize
Bring up
Bring up a muscle
A specialization phase: pick up to two lagging muscles. They get 2 extra sets a week and are trained first in each session, while you're freshest. To keep recovery in check, your other big muscles drop 1 set a week, never below the minimum that maintains them. Run it for a block or two, then rotate to the next weak point.
Lifts
Your lifts
Each lift's estimated max comes from your heaviest set each session, adjusted for how many reps you had left. The weekly rate is a trend line through your last 8 sessions of that lift, it's what the workout plan uses to decide how hard to push you on that movement. Deload weeks are left out so they don't drag the trend down.

Questions

How do I get in?

Request an invite above. We let people in from the waitlist in small groups and email you a link that fills in your code. If your coach uses FOREVER, their code gets you in straight away.

What does being a Founder mean?

Everyone who joins during the closed beta is a Founder. You get every feature, including everything we add later, free for life. No trial, no card, no catch. In return we'd love your honest feedback, and there's a Report a bug button right in the menu.

What happens after the beta?

When FOREVER opens to everyone, new members pay $14.99 a month or $119 a year. Founders keep paying nothing.

Is FOREVER in the App Store?

Not yet. FOREVER installs from your browser and works like a regular app, with a home-screen icon, full screen and notifications. On iPhone, open it in Safari, tap Share, then Add to Home Screen. On Android, tap Install in Chrome.

Do I need a coach?

No. FOREVER coaches you on its own: it plans your training, progresses your weights and sets your calories. If you work with a coach, they can connect to your account and adjust your plan directly.

Can I bring my MyFitnessPal history?

Yes. Request your data export from MyFitnessPal, then pick the file in the app's menu under Import history. Your food log and weigh-ins come across, so your trends start with real data.

Is my data private?

Your logs are yours. We don't sell your data or use it for ads, and only a coach you choose to connect can see it. You can export or delete everything from inside the app. Read the Privacy Policy.

I'm a coach. What do my clients pay?

Nothing to FOREVER. Clients connected to a coach on an active plan use the app free, and you charge them the way you always have. Your plan is priced by how many clients you coach.
